content.text: Write a very long story about dragons and adventures

# The Dragon Who Stole the Horizon

## 1. The Morning the World Ended Early

On the morning the horizon disappeared, Mara was arguing with a fish.

“You cannot possibly be worth six copper,” she told it.

The fish lay on the counter with its mouth open, which Mara considered a weak defense.

“Eight copper,” said the fishmonger.

“You said six.”

“That was before you insulted him.”

Mara had just decided that breakfast was a luxury for the morally weak when every bell in the harbor began to ring.

Not one bell after another, as they did for fires or funerals. All at once.

The bell above the lighthouse. The cracked bell at the customs house. The twelve little bells sewn into Old Renn’s coat. Even the bell at the bottom of the harbor, which had gone down with the *Saint Oriole* sixty-three years earlier.

People stopped.

Then they turned toward the sea.

Beyond the fishing boats, beyond the white-backed waves and the line of gulls following the morning trawlers, the world ended.

There was no horizon.

Sea and sky did not meet. They stopped at the edge of a vast gray emptiness, as if someone had taken a knife to a painting and cut away everything beyond the bay.

A fishing boat reached that emptiness.

For one dreadful moment it balanced there, its bow extending into nothing.

Then it vanished.

No splash. No scream.

Just gone.

The fishmonger crossed himself in three different religious traditions.

Mara dropped her last two copper coins.

High overhead, something enormous passed across the sun.

She saw wings first: dark blue, wide enough to cover the harbor. Then a body like a mountain seen underwater, a long tail, and seven horns sweeping backward from a narrow skull.

A dragon.

It flew inland carrying a bright golden line between its teeth.

The line bent and trembled.

It stretched from one end of the sky to the other.

Mara knew, with the strange certainty that comes before panic, that the dragon was carrying the horizon.

Then the creature disappeared behind the northern hills.

For three heartbeats, nobody spoke.

After that, everyone spoke at once.

Mara ran.

Not away from the sea. Not toward the town hall, where people would gather to shout questions at men who had never answered one honestly in their lives.

She ran toward the crooked tower at the end of Lantern Street.

Toward her grandfather.

And toward the map that had begun whispering her name the night before.

---

Grandfather Iven was standing on a chair when she burst into his workshop.

This was never a good sign.

At seventy-three, he considered ladders an admission of defeat. He had one boot on the seat, another on the backrest, and a broom in his hand. Above him, something moved inside the chimney.

“Close the door,” he said.

“The horizon’s gone.”

“Yes. Close the door.”

“A dragon took it.”

“Very inconsiderate. Door, Mara.”

She slammed it.

Something black shot from the chimney.

It struck the ceiling, knocked down three star charts, and landed in a bowl of ink.

For a moment Mara thought it was a crow.

Then it lifted its head.

It had copper-colored eyes, two crooked horns, and a face that looked deeply offended by the world.

It was a dragon.

A very small dragon.

Black ink ran from its wings.

“Oh,” it said. “Excellent. Witnesses.”

Mara stared.

Her grandfather climbed carefully down from the chair.

“Take the map,” he told her.

“Why is there a dragon in the ink?”

“Because your grandfather attempted murder with a broom,” said the dragon.

“It was a gentle discouragement.”

“You shouted, ‘I’ll stuff you and use you as a doorstop.’”

“I was improvising.”

Mara looked from one to the other.

Outside, the bells kept ringing.

“Grandfather.”

He stopped smiling.

That frightened her more than the missing horizon.

Iven crossed the workshop and lifted a cloth from the long table beneath the window.

The map underneath was older than the town, perhaps older than the kingdom. Its edges were dark with age. Rivers wandered across its surface when nobody was watching. Mountains rose and settled like sleeping animals.

In its center stood a city drawn in silver ink.

Mara had never seen it before.

Last night the map had shown only forests.

Now, beneath the city, letters formed.

**THE NINTH HOUR APPROACHES.**

The little dragon climbed from the ink bowl.

“Oh,” he said quietly.

“You know what that means?” Mara asked.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“It means I should have stayed in the chimney.”

Grandfather placed both hands on Mara’s shoulders.

“Listen carefully. The dragon you saw is called Orun. He is the Keeper of Distances.”

“He stole the horizon.”

“He moved it. There’s a difference.”

“A fishing boat disappeared.”

Iven’s jaw tightened.

“Then we have less time than I hoped.”

He took a brass compass from his pocket. Its needle spun once, twice, and pointed directly at Mara.

“This belonged to your mother.”

Mara went still.

Her mother had vanished eleven years earlier while charting the mountains beyond the northern kingdoms. Iven rarely spoke of her. When he did, it was as if he were walking across thin ice.

“What does she have to do with this?”

“Everything.”

From outside came a heavy crash.

The workshop windows rattled.

In the street, a horse screamed.

The little dragon scrambled under the table.

“Armored men,” he said. “I dislike armored men. They’re so often full of knives.”

Iven thrust the compass into Mara’s hand.

“Take the map. Go through the cellar. Find the city of Aster. Find your mother.”

Mara could not move.

“My mother is alive?”

The front door shook beneath a fist.

“IVEN VALE!” shouted someone outside. “BY ORDER OF THE CROWN!”

Her grandfather rolled up the map.

“I believe she is.”

“Then you should have told me.”

“Yes,” he said.

There was no excuse in his voice. Somehow that made it worse.

The door shook again.

Iven put the map in her arms.

“You can be angry with me when you return.”

“You’re coming.”

“I’ll delay them.”

“You can’t—”

“Mara.” He squeezed her hand. “Your mother always said a map was not a picture of the world. It was a promise that somewhere could be reached.”

The lock splintered.

Iven looked under the table.

“You too, sootling.”

The small dragon poked out his head.

“I have a name.”

“Then tell her on the way.”

Mara grabbed the dragon around the middle and ran for the cellar.

Behind her, she heard her grandfather greet the men at the door.

“Good morning, gentlemen. If this is about the taxes, I can explain almost everything.”

Then the cellar door slammed shut.

## 2. A Dragon of Modest Inconvenience

The tunnel beneath the workshop smelled of salt, mold, and old secrets.

Mara knew the first twenty steps. Her grandfather kept jars of pears there, along with two broken clocks and a sword he claimed was a curtain rod.

She had not known about the twenty-first step.

Or the hundred after it.

Or the underground river.

“This family,” she muttered.

The dragon wriggled out of her arms and landed on a damp stone.

“For the record, I object to being carried like laundry.”

“What’s your name?”

“Peregrine Ash-of-the-Last-Ember, Descendant of the Furnace Kings, Eater of—”

“Pip.”

“No.”

“Fine. Walk faster, Peregrine Ash-of-the-Last-Ember, Descendant of the Furnace Kings.”

“Pip will do in emergencies.”

The tunnel opened onto a narrow landing. A boat waited in the dark water, tied to an iron ring.

Inside lay a lantern, two blankets, a sack of food, and a note.

Mara recognized her grandfather’s handwriting.

*If you are reading this, something has gone terribly wrong.*

Below that:

*Or you have found the pears again. If so, leave some for winter.*

Her throat tightened.

She pushed the boat into the current.

Pip perched at the bow while Mara lit the lantern.

The river carried them beneath the town. Above, faint through earth and stone, came the rumble of carts and shouting.

For a while neither spoke.

Then Mara said, “Why were you in our chimney?”

“Hiding.”

“From the armored men?”

“Among other things.”

“Why?”

Pip examined one ink-stained claw.

“I may have escaped from a royal collection.”

“A zoo?”

“A prison with descriptive plaques.”

Mara looked at him more carefully. Beneath the ink, his scales were dark red rather than black. A pale band circled his neck where a collar had rubbed them away.

“What were they keeping you for?”

“Experiments. Displays. Questions about where larger dragons sleep.”

“Did you tell them?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He looked back at her.

“You say that very easily.”

“My grandfather taught me not to give bullies directions.”

The river curved. Ahead, a pale oval of daylight appeared.

Mara unrolled the map.

Its silver city glimmered.

A red line ran north through a forest, across a blank stretch labeled **THE UNREMEMBERED ROAD**, and into a mountain range.

On the bottom edge, words appeared.

**NINE DAYS UNTIL THE LAST DISTANCE CLOSES.**

“Nine days,” she whispered.

Pip leaned over the map.

“Oh, that’s not good.”

“Stop saying things are not good and tell me what’s happening.”

He folded his wings.

“There are old places in the world where everything is fastened together. Sea to shore. Morning to evening. Here to there. Aster is one of them.”

“A knot.”

“A very complicated knot. Dragons tend it.”

“And something’s wrong with it?”

“Something is cutting it.”

The boat slid into daylight.

They emerged beneath a curtain of willow branches. Behind them lay Bellweather, its harbor bells still ringing. Ahead stretched the low green country of the north.

Above the distant hills, Mara saw a thin golden thread.

The stolen horizon.

She took up the oars.

“Then we go to Aster.”

Pip settled on the sack of food.

“Yes. An excellent plan. Cross half a kingdom, find a city missing for a thousand years, and persuade creatures the size of fortresses not to eat us.”

Mara began to row.

“Can you breathe fire?”

“Certainly.”

“That might help.”

Pip inhaled.

His chest swelled.

He opened his jaws.

A small puff of warm smoke drifted out.

After a moment, he added, “It’s more impressive in cold weather.”

## 3. The Forest That Collected Names

By sunset, the river had narrowed into a stream.

By moonrise, the stream had become a series of muddy disagreements.

Mara dragged the boat ashore beneath a stone bridge and made camp.

She was seventeen years old. Until that morning, her greatest adventure had been climbing the lighthouse during a thunderstorm to prove that the keeper’s ghost was actually a goat.

Now the world was falling apart, her grandfather was under arrest, and her mother might be alive in a city that did not exist.

Pip ate three strips of dried meat and most of a pear.

“Do dragons usually eat fruit?” Mara asked.

“Do humans usually ask personal questions at dinner?”

She wrapped herself in a blanket.

When she finally slept, she dreamed of her mother.

Not as she remembered her: a woman with wind-tangled hair and ink on her thumbs, lifting Mara onto a windowsill to watch a storm.

In the dream, her mother stood behind a silver door.

She was holding it shut.

Something on the other side was knocking.

---

The forest began at noon the next day.

There was no gradual thickening of trees. One side of the road lay in warm sunlight, bordered by fields. On the other stood enormous white trunks beneath a roof of black leaves.

A wooden sign leaned beside the path.

**WELCOME TO THE KING’S WOOD.**

Someone had scratched out *KING’S*.

Beneath it, in smaller letters, was written:

**DO NOT ANSWER WHEN CALLED.**

Pip stopped.

“Ah.”

Mara looked at him.

“You know this place?”

“By reputation.”

“What does it do?”

“Collects names.”

“What does that mean?”

“If something calls your name and you answer, it takes it.”

“And then?”

“Then you don’t have one.”

Mara waited.

Pip sighed.

“Names attach us to ourselves. Lose yours, and other things begin to slip. Memories. Promises. Eventually your face.”

She pulled her scarf higher.

“Then we don’t answer.”

They entered the wood.

At first, it was almost beautiful.

Blue mushrooms glowed at the roots of the trees. Thin streams ran uphill through the moss. Birds with glassy wings moved soundlessly between branches.

Then Mara heard her grandfather.

“Mara?”

The voice came from just beyond a fallen trunk.

She stopped so abruptly Pip struck her heel.

“Mara, help me.”

She took one step.

Pip bit her ankle.

Pain flashed up her leg.

She gasped and clapped a hand over her mouth.

Between the trees stood a shape wearing her grandfather’s coat.

Its head was turned away.

Too far away.

Almost backward.

Mara walked on.

The voice followed.

First her grandfather.

Then the fishmonger.

Then her mother.

That was worst.

“Little star?”

Mara had not heard those words for eleven years.

Tears blurred the trees.

Pip pressed against her boot.

She kept walking.

They found the knight near the center of the forest.

He hung upside down from a branch, wrapped from ankles to chest in living roots. His armor was rusted. A yellow flower grew from the slit in his helmet.

When Mara approached, he lifted one gauntleted hand.

“Don’t suppose,” he said, “you have a knife?”

“Do you have a name?”

“Probably.”

“Probably?”

“Mislaid it.”
